_note: Two of the checks assert ABSENCES, because that is what an admission policy produces: no Route in the DEV namespace, and no unsized Deployment in PROD. On a cluster without Kyverno (or with the policy not Ready) both would find the object present and fail loudly, which is the correct signal — the lab would be teaching something untrue there. The Kyverno ClusterPolicy is created per session by session.objects and scoped to this session's two namespaces by label, so concurrent sessions cannot collide. The refused applies use `|| true` so the plan continues past an expected failure. The learner never reads the ClusterPolicy: it is cluster-scoped and Forbidden to a tenant (measured). The lab asserts that boundary instead, and proves the policy exists through the refusals it produces — each of which names the rule.

steps.run: oc auth can-i list clusterpolicies || true
envsubst < hello-dcs-unsized.yaml | oc apply -f - -n $DEV_NS && oc rollout status deploy/hello-dcs -n $DEV_NS --timeout=180s
envsubst < hello-dcs-sized.yaml | oc apply -f - -n $PROD_NS && oc rollout status deploy/hello-dcs -n $PROD_NS --timeout=180s
oc apply -f service.yaml -n $PROD_NS && oc apply -f route.yaml -n $PROD_NS

oc get deploy hello-dcs -n $DEV_NS -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\n"}'; oc get deploy hello-dcs -n $PROD_NS -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\n"}'
